twins.question: In ridge regression, what happens to the learned weights as the regularisation strength λ increases?
options: They grow larger to fit the data better
They shrink towards zero
They are not affected by λ
They all become exactly zero once λ > 1
twins.explanation: Ridge adds λ‖w‖² to the loss. A larger λ makes big weights more expensive, so the best solution moves towards smaller weights. They shrink towards zero but usually don't become exactly zero; that is lasso's behaviour.
hints: Look at the extra term ridge adds to the loss. What does it punish?
If λ makes that punishment stronger, how would the weights change to keep the total loss low?

twins.question: A ridge regression model is underfitting: both training and test error are high. Which change is most likely to help?
options: Increase λ
Increase λ and remove some features
Decrease λ
Keep λ and train for more epochs
twins.explanation: Underfitting means the model is too constrained. In ridge, λ is what constrains the weights. Lowering λ lets the weights take larger values so the model can fit the data more closely.
hints: Underfitting means the model is held back too much. Which part of ridge holds it back?
If λ controls how strongly the weights are held back, which direction loosens that hold?

twins.question: In k-nearest neighbours classification, what typically happens to the decision boundary as k increases from 1 to a larger value?
options: It becomes more jagged and overfits more
It stays exactly the same
It becomes smoother
It disappears because neighbours are ignored
twins.explanation: With k = 1 each prediction copies the single closest point, so the boundary bends around every training point. A larger k takes a vote over more neighbours, which averages out noise and gives a smoother boundary.
hints: With k = 1, how many training points decide each prediction?
What happens to the effect of one noisy point when many neighbours vote together?

twins.question: A 1-nearest-neighbour classifier gets 100% training accuracy but poor test accuracy. What is the usual first fix?
options: Increase k
Keep k = 1 and add more features
Duplicate every training point
Use a smaller training set
twins.explanation: Perfect training accuracy with poor test accuracy is overfitting. With k = 1 the model follows every noisy point. Increasing k makes each prediction a vote of several neighbours, which reduces this variance.
hints: Perfect training accuracy but poor test accuracy: what is that problem called?
Which setting of k makes a single noisy neighbour matter less?

twins.question: What is the entropy of a decision-tree node where every sample belongs to the same class?
options: It depends on the number of samples
twins.explanation: Entropy measures how mixed the classes in a node are. If every sample is the same class there is no uncertainty at all: −1 × log₂(1) = 0.
hints: Entropy measures uncertainty. How uncertain are you about the class of a sample from this node?
Try the formula with one class that has probability 1. What is log₂(1)?

twins.question: A split produces a child node containing only 'yes' samples. How should that child's impurity be described?
options: Maximum impurity, because all samples agree
Zero impurity, it is a pure node
Half impurity, because there are two classes in the problem
Undefined, because one class is missing
twins.explanation: Impurity measures how mixed a node is. A node holding only one class is not mixed at all, so its entropy (and Gini impurity) is zero. This is exactly what a good split aims for.
hints: Impurity measures how mixed the classes in a node are. How mixed is this node?
If you picked any sample from this node, how sure would you be of its class?
